content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Explain how ultrafiltration occurs in the glomerulus
Describe what is filtered and what is not
Explain the role of blood pressure in filtration

is the first stage of urine formation. It occurs in the glomerulus where high blood pressure forces small molecules out of the blood and into the Bowman's capsule. Large molecules like proteins and blood cells remain in the blood.
Filtration under pressure that separates small molecules from large ones
Formation of glomerular filtrate (like blood plasma but without proteins)
Blood enters glomerulus under high pressure
Small molecules forced through capillary walls
Afferent arteriole wider than efferent arteriole
Blood enters faster than it can leave
About 50% higher than in normal capillaries
Contains all small molecules from blood
But only 1-2 litres of urine produced
Allows fine control of what's kept
The kidney selectively filters waste only
All small molecules are filtered; useful ones reabsorbed later
Proteins are actively removed from filtrate
Filtrate is the same as urine
Filtrate is modified extensively before becoming urine
Low blood pressure doesn't affect kidneys
Pressure-driven filtration separating small from large molecules
Knot of capillaries where filtration occurs
Cells with foot-like processes forming filtration barrier
Layers that determine what is filtered
High pressure created by narrow efferent arteriole
Three-layer barrier: endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes
Small molecules filtered: water, glucose, amino acids, urea, salts
Large molecules NOT filtered: proteins, blood cells
Non-selective filtration followed by selective reabsorption
